name: Moravec's Paradox
aliases: Moravec's paradox in AI and robotics
statement: For machines, high-level reasoning is easy and a toddler's perception and movement are hard.
meaning: Moravec's paradox is the observation that, contrary to intuition, the abstract reasoning humans find hard — chess, logic, calculation — takes relatively little computation to reproduce in machines, while the sensorimotor skills a one-year-old performs effortlessly — seeing, walking, grasping, recognising faces — demand enormous computation and remain extraordinarily difficult. In Hans Moravec's words, it is comparatively easy to make computers perform at adult level on intelligence tests or at checkers, and difficult or impossible to give them the perceptual and motor skills of a one-year-old.
mechanism: The explanation is evolutionary. Sensorimotor abilities are the product of hundreds of millions to a billion years of selection, honed and compiled into fast, unconscious neural machinery so efficient that it feels effortless — and so deeply buried that we have little introspective access to how it works, making it hard to reverse-engineer. Abstract reasoning, by contrast, is evolutionarily recent, performed slowly and consciously, and so is a thin, inspectable layer that is comparatively easy to encode. What feels hard to us is computationally shallow; what feels effortless is computationally vast, so the difficulty ordering for machines is roughly the reverse of our intuition.

examples.text: Machines reached superhuman play in chess and later Go decades before robots could reliably pick up and manipulate ordinary objects in a cluttered room.

Moravec wrote that the sensory and motor brain encodes a billion years of experience, and that reasoning is the thinnest veneer of human thought, effective only because it rests on that older, unconscious base.
Steven Pinker summarised the lesson that the main finding of thirty-five years of AI is that the hard problems are easy and the easy problems are hard.

variants.name: Minsky's version
variants.text: Marvin Minsky's related point that we are least aware of what our minds do best, so the skills hardest to reverse-engineer are the ones that run flawlessly below conscious awareness.

variants.name: Brooks's embodied turn
variants.text: Rodney Brooks's response in robotics: build intelligence from sensing and action rather than abstract reasoning, taking the paradox as a reason to start with the body, not the intellect.

whyItMatters: It reframed expectations in artificial intelligence and robotics, explaining why symbolic reasoning fell to machines early while perception and dexterity lagged for decades, and why robotics is hard in ways the public underestimates. It guides where effort and humility are warranted, warns against equating fluent reasoning with general competence, and remains a useful lens on why today's systems can argue and calculate while reliable physical manipulation stays stubbornly difficult.

working.text: expect tasks that feel intellectually hard to humans to be relatively tractable for machines, and tasks that feel effortless to be computationally deep.
budget for perception, movement, and manipulation as genuinely hard problems rather than assuming they follow easily once reasoning is solved.
treat the paradox as a durable observation whose exact line moves as deep learning narrows some perception gaps, not as a fixed law.

limits: It is an observation and generalisation, not a formal law with a precise measure or proof. Its boundary shifts: modern deep learning has narrowed some perception gaps — machine vision and speech recognition among them — even as broad physical dexterity remains hard, so some argue the paradox is being partly eroded. The evolutionary explanation is plausible and widely accepted but is an interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism. It is best read as a heuristic that captured a real and lasting pattern in AI, with the details of where the easy-hard line falls always subject to revision.
misreadings: It does not say machines cannot do sensorimotor tasks — only that these are far harder to engineer than the reasoning tasks that seem impressive to us. It is not a precise law but an observation, so exact thresholds and its current boundary are matters of judgement. And it is not obsolete: although perception has advanced, general dexterity and robust real-world manipulation still lag reasoning, which is the pattern the paradox names.
origin: Articulated in the 1980s by Hans Moravec, with related observations by Marvin Minsky and Rodney Brooks; Moravec's canonical statement appears in his book 'Mind Children' (1988).

sources.text: Moravec's paradox, Wikipedia. — Moravec's one-year-old quote, the evolutionary explanation, and the Minsky, Brooks, and Pinker statements.
Moravec, Mind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence (Harvard University Press, 1988). — the original formulation and the 'thinnest veneer' passage.
